title: Checkpoint: Moving Pictures
objective: After this level you can explain how inventors turned photographs into projected moving pictures that could tell a story.
summary: Early films were copyrighted as photographic prints on paper, which is why many survive in the Library of Congress's Paper Print Collection. The chapter traced still frames to projected stories.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: some of the first movies survive as rolls of paper.
cards.body: This whole chapter has said that a film is still pictures in disguise. Early filmmakers proved it in the last place you'd expect: a copyright office. Here's how, plus the chapter's story in one line.

events.label: Muybridge's 12 cameras catch a galloping horse
The first Kinetoscope parlor opens in New York
The Lumières' paid screening at the Grand Café, Paris
Méliès's A Trip to the Moon

cards.headline: Films saved as photographs on paper
cards.body: Film companies often copied each other's films. To protect its own, from October 1896 the Edison Company regularly registered films for copyright, sending them to the Library of Congress as photographic prints on paper rolls. The earliest surviving copyrighted film, a sneeze recorded on January 7, 1894, arrived as a series of photo prints. These paper prints form the Library's Paper Print Collection, and The Great Train Robbery is among them.

mascot.line: It connects: a film is still frames, so a stack of photographs could stand in for it. Level 1's idea, saving film history.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one breath
cards.body: Still frames, shown fast, become motion because your brain supplies it through beta movement. Muybridge sliced a gallop into stills; Edison's lab put film in a peephole box; the Lumières projected it for a paying crowd; Méliès made it magic; Porter cut it into a story. And a projector's intermittent movement holds each frame still, at the standard of 24 frames a second.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: How still photographs, shown fast, became projected movies that could tell a story.
Why your brain sees motion in still frames, and why persistence of vision is the old answer.
What a projector's claw and shutter do, and why sound films settled on 24 frames a second.
Who turned film into a crowd event, a magic show and a story: the Lumières, Méliès and Porter.

questions.prompt: Why did the Edison Company send its films to the Library of Congress as paper prints?

options.label: To register copyright and protect them from copying
To sell them as souvenir photo books
options.rationale: They were deposits for copyright, not products.

options.label: Because paper was cheaper to project than film
To help the Lumières make copies
options.rationale: The aim was to stop copying.

questions.explanation: Companies copied each other's films, so Edison registered films for copyright as photographic prints on paper.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: which effect makes flickering light look steady, as opposed to turning stills into motion?

options.label: Apparent motion
options.rationale: That's the effect that creates movement.

options.label: Beta movement
options.rationale: That's a kind of apparent motion.

options.label: Flicker fusion
The stop trick
options.rationale: That's Méliès's camera trick, not perception.

questions.explanation: Flicker fusion makes flickering light look steady; apparent motion turns still images into movement.

questions.prompt: Why could a paper roll of photographs stand in for a film in the copyright office?

options.label: Because early films had no pictures, only titles
Because a film is a series of still photographs
Because paper prints could be played on a projector
options.rationale: They were records, not projection copies.

options.label: Because the law banned film stock in libraries
options.rationale: Nothing in this chapter says so.

questions.explanation: A film is still photographs shown in rapid succession, so printing its frames on paper preserves every picture.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: a bus turned into a hearse and a queen into a dummy. Which trick did both use?

options.label: Cross-cutting between places
A twin-bladed shutter
options.rationale: That's a projector part, not a trick.

options.label: Hand-cranking faster
The stop trick

questions.explanation: Stop the camera, swap what's in front of it, restart: Méliès's bus and Edison's 1895 beheading scene both used it.

questions.prompt: The Lumières' Cinématographe (Level 6) was also a projector. How did it pull film past the lamp (Level 9)?

options.label: On a continuous loop, like the Kinetoscope
options.rationale: The Kinetoscope's film ran continuously; the Lumières' stopped and started.

options.label: With claws, moving and pausing like a sewing machine
By hand, one frame at a time with tweezers
options.rationale: A crank turned a cam that drove claws.

options.label: With twelve separate cameras in a row

questions.explanation: A cam drove claws through the perforations, advancing the film and holding it still, much like a sewing machine.
